extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, literary criticism, and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging poetry and the imitative arts from the standpoint of Plato's Tenth Book and subsequent critical commentary — focusing on truth, knowledge, moral/political effects, and educational usefulness. Useful for assessing whether particular works of poetry/Drama should be permitted, censured, or valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitator thrice removed from the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (and painter) is an imitator and therefore 'thrice removed' from the original truth: God (the maker of forms) → craftsman (carpenter) → painter/poet (image-maker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the poet imitates appearances of things rather than the real forms, his creations are only images of images and cannot capture absolute truth. Example: the painter paints not the original bed but the carpenter's bed; the tragic poet is 'thrice removed' from truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation lacks knowledge (no scientia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is devoid of knowledge, being only a kind of play or sport; the imitator has only appearance, not science or true opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet can represent an art (e.g., a cobbler) without understanding its practice; thus imitation does not qualify as genuine knowledge and cannot reliably instruct in practical arts or truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be useful as well as delightful
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must show that it is useful as well as delightful before being admitted; entertainment alone is insufficient grounds for cultural authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's prescription: allow poetry only if it defends itself in verse and can demonstrate usefulness (e.g., hymns to the gods or praise of great men). Otherwise, poetry that simply pleases but misleads or weakens virtue should be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets cannot be reliable educators of the city
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets (e.g., Homer) have not supplied laws, inventions, or ways of life that govern cities; therefore they are not true educators of a polis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from historical example: if Homer really educated Hellas he would have had devoted followers and legislative influence; his lack of such practical civic influence undermines the claim that poets impart usable knowledge for governing life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative arts excite and corrupt the emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama injuriously excite the feelings, encouraging indulgence in sorrow or coarse merriment which would be censured in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathizing with another's grief or laughing at stage buffoonery can habituate inappropriate emotional responses in private life. Thus poetry 'feeds and waters the passions' and can let desires rule rather than reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art concerns particulars, not universals (inferior to philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and other imitative arts deal with particulars of sense, while philosophy deals with universals and therefore attains a higher truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's hierarchy: the higher faculties of the soul grasp universals; the lower (sense and imagination) grasp particulars. Hence poetry's subject-matter situates it on an inferior cognitive level compared to philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry lacks a 'measure of greater and less' (no normative metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets have 'no measure of greater and less' and therefore should not have authority over the mind of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poets cannot properly discriminate degrees (of value, truth, morality) by rule and measure, their authority in shaping citizens' minds is epistemically and ethically suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative arts are subject to inevitable compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitative art sacrifices some exactness for the sake of representation and some ideal truth for the sake of sense; they are necessarily compromises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the trade-off: representation gains immediacy and feeling but loses some claim to ideal or abstract truth; evaluators should judge works by how they balance these losses and gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry can ennoble and embody the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Against Plato: art may ennoble ordinary subjects and give them an ideal interest — conveying something beyond mere imitation (examples: Rembrandt's mills, Turner's ship hulls, Pheidias' Zeus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work transcends mere appearance to express an ideal or divine quality. If it does, it may partake of a higher truth and thereby justify its aesthetic and moral value despite Plato's imitation objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art may harmonize rather than enervate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts may have the effect of harmonizing the soul as well as enervating it; they can 'present thought in the form of feeling' and enlist emotions on the side of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poem/play, consider whether it cultivates higher emotions (consolation, elevation, courage, resignation) that support reason and virtue rather than merely indulging base impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's catharsis claim vs. indulgence objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's theory: tragedy purges passions by pity and fear; Plato rejects this, seeing only indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sensible evaluation weighs whether the work effects purification of emotions (therapeutic expression) or merely provides safe indulgence that weakens moral self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's political/corrupting alignment (friends of tyrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets can be complicit in political corruption, flattering tyrants and serving as false teachers or propagandists for despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poet's political role and patronage: does the work legitimize oppression or supply 'false ideas' that strengthen tyranny? This factor bears on whether poetry should be admitted into a just state.

rubrics_metrics.name: The actor's profession can degrade the actor's character
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting (playing many parts) may destroy a performer's stable self; the actor becomes the slave of art and may lose personal integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theatrical practice, consider moral effects on practitioners as well as audiences — whether performing in certain roles habitually undermines character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual value: poetry's place varies by age
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's cultural value differs across historical stages (infancy of mankind vs. later ages); what counts as central literature in one era may be marginal in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments of poetry should account for historical function: early societies relied on poetry as primary intellectual culture; in other periods prose, science, or law may supplant some poetic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should cultivate judgment to choose the good life
rubrics_metrics.description: Education's aim is to teach a man to refuse the evil and choose the good by knowing the combinations of life (beauty with poverty/wealth, knowledge with external goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literature by whether it contributes to this practical moral knowledge — whether it helps readers judge life-choices and to prefer the life that 'makes men better.' Literary works that aid this aim earn educational merit.
